> Luna will be a little robot character with purple hair, white armor, and a pink heart. I want her to react to what is happening on the computer instead of playing the same animation all the time. When the PC is quiet, she could rest or look around. When it is working harder, she could switch to a running or working animation. Finishing a study session could trigger a small celebration. If the computer stops sending data, the display should show that it is disconnected instead of leaving old numbers on the screen. The character will use prepared 2D animation frames with a rendered 3D look. I am not planning to render a full 3D model on the ESP32 or add a chatbot in the first version.

## Design

### 2026-11-01: I started Luna Desk by working on the Python side of the project in VS Code. I created a virtual environment and used psutil to read my computer’s CPU and RAM usage. The program packages those reading

**7h**

I started Luna Desk by working on the Python side of the project in VS Code. I created a virtual environment and used psutil to read my computer’s CPU and RAM usage. The program packages those readings into JSON messages, including a timestamp and a character state. Luna switches to “working” when CPU usage reaches 30% and stays “idle” below that threshold.

Next, I added serial communication with pySerial. Since I do not have the display board yet, I tested the connection code using software loopback. The program sends a packet, reads it back, and checks whether the received data matches the original message. This let me check the message format and software serial round trip before testing with physical hardware.

I also built a desktop preview with Tkinter to try the interface. It includes live statistics, a clock, navigation buttons, and a 25-minute focus timer with start, pause, and reset controls. I added Luna’s idle and working animations, but the first playback attempt showed incomplete frames. Using Pillow to reconstruct the GIF frames before displaying them fixed that problem.

Finally, I added a demo option to force either animation without changing the real CPU and RAM readings. I tested the preview on my PC and pushed the code to GitHub. Communication with the actual ESP32 board is still pending.

### 2026-11-01: At this stage, I finished the planned software and CAD work for Luna Desk. The desktop preview runs on my PC, the ESP32-S3 firmware compiles, and the enclosure files are ready for a first print. Testi

**15h**

At this stage, I finished the planned software and CAD work for Luna Desk. The desktop preview runs on my PC, the ESP32-S3 firmware compiles, and the enclosure files are ready for a first print. Testing with the physical board is still pending because I do not have it yet.

In Arduino IDE, I adapted Waveshare’s display and touch example into Luna Desk’s interface. I added the CPU and RAM dashboard, usage bars, a clock, and navigation to a 25-minute focus timer with start, pause, and reset controls. The firmware receives JSON messages from the PC program and checks the incoming values before updating the screen. If valid messages stop arriving for five seconds, it clears the old readings and displays a disconnected status.

I also integrated Luna’s idle and working animations into the firmware. The frames are stored in program flash, so this version does not require a microSD card. The completed sketch compiled successfully, using about 50% of the selected application partition.

For the mechanical design, I used Onshape and the manufacturer’s reference model to create a front shell and removable rear cover. I added board mounting columns, closure bosses for M2 heat-set inserts, and openings for USB, the existing buttons, and microSD access. One closure boss initially obstructed the USB opening, so I moved it sideways to clear the cable path. Section views helped me inspect the internal arrangement.

Finally, I designed a separate desk stand with two support ribs at 60 degrees and a lower retaining stop. I exported the STEP files, added the converted STL files and screenshots to GitHub, and completed the README and planning BOM. The next phase is to receive the board, test the firmware on hardware, and check the fit and stability of the printed parts.
